title: United Food & Commercial Workers Union Local 751 v. Brown Group, Inc. (1996)
shortTitle: United Food & Commercial Workers Union Local 751 v. Brown Group, Inc.
summary: The third prong of the Hunt test for associational standing, which bars an association from seeking damages for its members, is prudential, so Congress may authorize a union to sue for its members' backpay.
notes:
Key line: "But once an association has satisfied Hunt's first and second prongs assuring adversarial vigor in pursuing a claim for which member Article III standing exists, it is difficult to see a constitutional necessity for anything more." Justice Souter, for the Court.

Citation: 517 U.S. 544 (1996).

sections.Parties: Petitioner was United Food and Commercial Workers Union Local 751, the exclusive bargaining representative of workers at a shoe plant. Respondent was Brown Group, Inc., doing business as Brown Shoe Co., which operated the plant. The United States appeared as amicus curiae supporting the union. The union sued under the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act (WARN Act) to recover backpay owed to each of its members affected by the plant closing.
sections.Material Facts: The WARN Act requires employers to give workers or their union 60 days' notice before a plant closing or mass layoff and allows aggrieved employees or their representatives to sue for backpay for each day of violation. On March 20, 1992, Brown Shoe wrote to a representative of the international union stating that it would close its Dixon, Missouri plant and permanently lay off 277 employees beginning that day. The local union alleged that the company had in fact begun the layoffs before sending the letter and had continued them through February and March without giving the required notice. The union sought 60 days of backpay for each affected member. The company argued that the union lacked standing because each member would have to participate in the suit to prove individual damages.
sections.Procedural History: The union sued in the Eastern District of Missouri. The District Court dismissed the complaint under Rule 12(b)(6), reasoning that claims for money damages on behalf of members necessarily require the members' participation. The Eighth Circuit affirmed in 1995, holding that the union could not satisfy the third prong of the Hunt test and therefore lacked associational standing. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on February 20, 1996, and on May 13, 1996 reversed and remanded.
sections.Issue: Hunt v. Washington State Apple Advertising Commission allows an association to sue for its members when the members would have standing, the interests are germane to the association's purpose, and neither the claim nor the relief requires the participation of individual members. Courts had read the third prong to bar associational suits for money damages. The WARN Act authorizes a union to sue for backpay on behalf of its members. May Congress override the third prong of the Hunt test by statute, or is that prong a constitutional requirement of Article III that bars the union's damages suit?
sections.Holding: Yes. Hunt's first prong, requiring that at least one member have standing in his own right, is grounded in Article III, and the second prong, requiring germaneness, complements it. The third prong concerns administrative convenience and efficiency, not the elements of a case or controversy, and is therefore prudential and subject to abrogation by Congress. The WARN Act authorizes union suits for members' backpay, so the union has standing. The judgment was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Souter first confirmed, relying on North Star Steel Co. v. Thomas, that the WARN Act grants unions authority to sue for damages on behalf of members. He then analyzed the three prongs of Hunt v. Washington State Apple Advertising Commission. The requirement that a member have standing in his own right ensures that a genuine case or controversy exists and is constitutionally required. The germaneness requirement ensures the association has a stake and will be a proper adversary. Once those two requirements are met, it is difficult to see any constitutional need for more. The bar on damages suits reflects concerns about the difficulty of proving individual damages and the risk of inadequate representation, which are matters of judicial administration and efficiency. The Court found circumstantial evidence of the prong's prudential character in the many statutes and rules that let one person sue for another even when damages are sought, such as Title VII suits by the EEOC and the Fair Labor Standards Act. Because the third prong is prudential, Congress can remove it, and the WARN Act does so by authorizing a representative to sue for its members' backpay. The Court noted that a defendant remains protected because members' individual damages must still be proven in the ordinary way.

topics.lrs-n-standing-association: The case identifies Congress’s power to alter Hunt’s third requirement.
topics.lrs-n-standing-congress: Congress can remove a prudential requirement while Article III remains binding.
topics.lrs-n-standing-constitutional: The case sorts Hunt's three prongs into Article III requirements and prudential requirements Congress can abrogate.
